summary: Describes a straightforward format for writing concise yet descriptive MIB modules used in network management. It is an Internet standard.

plainLanguage.summary: This is a form with blanks for describing the things a network device can report about itself.

questions: what is the concise mib format
what is the mib object-type macro
what does the index clause do in a mib
how are rows added to an snmp table
subtitle: A single compact format that merges the prose and the formal definition of each network management object.

tldr.problem: MIB descriptions for SNMP-managed objects were written twice, once as prose and once as a formal ASN.1 definition, so they were redundant and easy to edit inconsistently.
tldr.mechanism: The memo extends the OBJECT-TYPE macro with DESCRIPTION, REFERENCE, INDEX and DEFVAL clauses so one definition carries everything, including how table rows are identified and created.
tldr.outcome: It states that all future MIB modules are intended to be written in this format, and it is an Internet Standard.

today: RFC 1212 is an Internet Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It states that all future MIB modules are intended to be written in this format.

sections.title: Where Concise MIBs Came From
sections.content:
The Internet's network management started with a two-prong strategy: the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) in the short term, and the OSI management framework to be examined in the long term. The Structure of Management Information (SMI) and the Management Information Base (MIB) were first designed to work with both.

Later the requirements of the two frameworks turned out to be more different than expected, so the compatibility requirement was suspended. That let the SNMP-based framework produce MIB-II. The SMI also defined three ways to add objects: new versions of the MIB, the experimental subtree and the enterprises subtree.

As more objects were defined through the experimental route, the descriptions turned out to contain redundant information. This memo suggests an enhancement that removes the redundancy and keeps the descriptive text.
sections.plainLanguage: People kept writing the same facts about each object twice. This memo is a way to write them just once.

sections.title: Conceptual Tables and Columnar Objects
sections.content:
SNMP operations apply only to scalar objects. For convenience, developers still imagine tables on top of the ordered set of MIB objects. A conceptual table has zero or more rows, and each row has one or more scalar columnar objects. The table and the row are each defined with the OBJECT-TYPE macro, with the ACCESS clause not-accessible.

At the protocol level, which objects belong to the same row is a matter of convention, not protocol. The memo gives a reason: a Get-Next request on the last columnar object of a row returns the next column of the first row, or the first object after the table, instead of an error. One exchange therefore tells the manager both that the row or table ended and what comes next.
sections.plainLanguage: A table is just a way of pretending the list of facts has rows and columns. The device does not know about rows, but people find them handy.

sections.title: Deleting and Adding Rows
sections.content:
To remove a row, MIB-II defines an integer columnar object for each row. A management station sets it to a value usually called invalid. Whether the agent then drops the entry is implementation specific, so managers must be ready to receive entries that are not in use and must check the status object to interpret them.

To add a row, a manager sends an SNMP set with variable bindings for instances the agent does not yet have. The memo lists three behaviors that are all conformant:

  • Reject the set with error-status noSuchName.
  • Accept it and create the named instances, answering badValue if a value or syntax is unacceptable.
  • Accept it, create the named instances, and also create supplemental instances to complete the row.

All three are fully acceptable, subject to access control and the definitions of the objects themselves.
sections.plainLanguage: To add or remove a line in a table, you ask the device with a special request. The device may say no, may add just what you asked, or may fill in the missing blanks for you.

sections.title: The Extended OBJECT-TYPE Macro
sections.content:
Before this memo, a MIB had two parts: a textual part grouping objects, and a MIB module that described them with the ASN.1 OBJECT-TYPE macro. The memo combines them by extending the macro. Each definition has these clauses:

  • SYNTAX (required): the abstract data structure, written in a restricted subset of ASN.1 for simplicity.
  • ACCESS (required): read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible. This is the minimum support required; implementations may allow more.
  • STATUS (required): mandatory, optional, obsolete or deprecated.
  • DESCRIPTION (optional, but required if the module has no textual description elsewhere): a quoted text carrying all semantics needed to implement the object.
  • REFERENCE (optional): a cross-reference to an object in another MIB module, useful when converting another organization's MIB.
  • INDEX and DEFVAL (optional): covered below.

The value of an invocation is the object's name, an object identifier. Macro expansion conceptually happens at implementation time, not at run time.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a form with labeled boxes: what kind of thing, who may touch it, is it required, and a short note about what it means.

sections.title: INDEX and DEFVAL: Naming and Defaults
sections.content:
The INDEX clause may appear only on an object that is a conceptual row. It names the object or objects whose values uniquely identify a row, which replaces the old section on identifying object instances. Without an INDEX clause, an instance of a non-columnar object is named by appending a sub-identifier of zero to the object's name.

The syntax of each index object decides how it becomes sub-identifiers: an integer is one sub-identifier, a fixed-length string takes one per octet, a variable-length string takes a length followed by one per octet, and an IpAddress takes four. MIB-II examples include ifEntry indexed by ifIndex and tcpConnEntry indexed by local address, local port, remote address and remote port.

The DEFVAL clause gives an acceptable default that an agent may use when it creates a row on its own (the third paradigm above) and the set did not supply that column. If no acceptable default exists, the objects in the INDEX clause must be read-write.
sections.plainLanguage: The index is the label that tells rows apart, like a student ID. The default is the answer the device writes in when you leave a blank empty.

sections.title: Worked Example: ipNetToMediaTable
sections.content:
The memo shows the MIB-II ipNetToMediaTable, which maps IP addresses to physical addresses, written in the new format. It uses a table object, a row object with INDEX { ipNetToMediaIfIndex, ipNetToMediaNetAddress }, a SEQUENCE listing the four columns, and one OBJECT-TYPE per column.

The ipNetToMediaType column takes other(1), invalid(2), dynamic(3) or static(4). Setting it to invalid(2) invalidates the entry, which shows the row deletion convention from earlier in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The example fills in the form for one real table, a phone book that matches network addresses to hardware addresses.

sections.title: De-osifying MIBs
sections.content:
The appendix explains how to convert a MIB defined by another organization into this format. Start with a skeleton module, then sort objects into groups. Groups are units of conformance: everything in a group is mandatory, and implementations support whole groups or none. It is wisest to ignore optional objects at first and define a core of essential ones.

A managed object class that can have only one instance maps to plain OBJECT-TYPE definitions. One that can have many becomes a conceptual table. As a rule of thumb a row should hold no more than approximately 20 objects, so it fits in one PDU.

Syntax maps simply: BOOLEAN becomes an INTEGER with true(1) or false(2), ENUMERATED becomes an INTEGER, and a BIT STRING of no more than 32 bits becomes an INTEGER defined as a sum, otherwise an OCTET STRING. Actions are modeled as read-write objects whose written value triggers the action.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone else wrote their list in a different style, here is how to copy it into this form without losing anything important.
